155.title: Holy days and the saints' calendar
155.hook: a few great feasts are kept like Sundays (the list varies by country)
155.tomorrow: Camp 3 close: a rule of life
155.howItsDone: Catholics go to Mass on Sundays and on their country's holy days of obligation, such as Christmas and All Saints; many also follow the saints' calendar, keeping name days, the feasts of their parish's patron and their own patron saints.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fifty days of Easter, and the alleluia coming back. Your line was longer than lent. Did you keep one celebration going? A new week, and the last full lesson of this camp. Day one hundred fifty-five.

Open a Catholic calendar, the kind that hangs in a parish hall, and look at any square. There's a name in it. March 19, Joseph. August 15, Mary taken up into heaven. November 1, all the saints at once. Then a random Tuesday in July, and there's still a name: some bishop, some farmer's daughter, some martyr from a city you've never heard of. Almost no day is empty. And a few of the squares carry a special mark, because on those days Catholics are asked to go to Mass, even on a Wednesday.
screen: `A NAME IN EVERY SQUARE.` → `A FEW SPECIALLY MARKED.`

segments.voice: Those marked days are holy days of obligation. Catholics are asked to go to Mass every Sunday, and on a handful of great feasts they're asked to do the same, whatever day of the week it falls on, and to rest from unnecessary work where they can. The Church's general law lists ten of these feasts, among them Christmas, the Epiphany, the Ascension, Mary the Mother of God, the Assumption, Saint Joseph, Peter and Paul, and All Saints. But it lets each country's bishops trim the list or move a feast to the nearest Sunday. So the list really does vary. In the United States the list is shorter, and some are lifted when they fall right next to a weekend. Ask a Catholic in Ireland or Italy and you'll get a different answer. Then there's everyone else on the calendar. The saints' days. The Church keeps a general calendar of saints for the whole world, and a much longer book, the Roman Martyrology, which lists saints and martyrs for every day of the year, often several on a single day. Here's the surprising part: a saint's feast is usually kept on the day they died, not the day they were born. The old Latin name for that day is dies natalis, birthday, because the Church thinks of it as their birthday into heaven. So every morning, somewhere, somebody is keeping a birthday for someone who died a long time ago. Parishes are named for them. Children are named for them. And in some Catholic families, a name day is kept like a second birthday.
screen: `MARKED DAYS: KEPT LIKE A SUNDAY.` · `THE LIST VARIES BY COUNTRY.` · `A SAINT FOR EVERY DAY.` · `THE DAY THEY DIED: A BIRTHDAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find today's saint. After the bell, look it up on any Catholic calendar, and pick one name. For now, settle and breathe, and think about the idea itself: that today already belongs to someone who lived a whole life and finished it. Think, too, of someone you knew who has died. What day was theirs? If you pray, you can ask today's saint to pray for you, or for them. If you don't, simply remember one life with gratitude. The bell holds the time.
Dies natalis. Latin for birthday, the day a saint died, kept as their birthday into heaven. Today's word.
Your line: every day belongs to someone. Today, find out whose day it is, and say their name once, to yourself or to someone else. Day one hundred fifty-five.

156.title: Camp 3 close: a rule of life
156.hook: a morning offering, a decade, the Angelus, an evening look back
156.howItsDone: Many Catholics keep a simple personal rule of life, such as a morning offering, the Angelus at noon, a decade of the rosary and an evening examination of conscience; some make it formal as oblates of a monastery or members of a lay third order.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the red days on the calendar and a saint's dies natalis in every square. Your line was every day belongs to someone. Whose day was it? Today, the last day of the practices. Day one hundred fifty-six.

This camp started at the church door: a first Mass, or a first in years. Since then you've been handed a lot. Holy water at the door. Knees and bows. The Glory Be, the Creed, the morning offering, the Angelus. The Mass scene by scene, from the Confiteor to the Sanctus to the sending. The rosary, a decade at a time. Seven sacraments. Confession up close, the tabernacle and its red lamp, the monstrance, the holy hour. Advent, ashes, stations, the Triduum and the Exsultet. That's far too much for anyone to do every day. Nobody does all of it. So what do people actually do?
screen: `SIXTY DAYS OF PRACTICES.` → `FAR TOO MUCH FOR ONE DAY.` → `SO WHAT DO PEOPLE DO?`

segments.voice: They keep a rule of life. The word rule sounds strict, but in Latin, regula first meant a straight stick, a ruler, the kind you use to draw a line or measure a wall. A rule of life is a measuring stick for your days, not a cage. One that has lasted was written by Saint Benedict for his monks, and Benedictine monasteries still live by it. It gives hours for prayer, for work, for reading, for meals and for sleep. And near the end, Benedict calls it a little rule for beginners. The man tradition calls the father of Western monks thought he'd written a starter kit. You don't have to be a monk. Plenty of lay Catholics keep a rule, some of them formally, as Benedictine oblates or lay Franciscans or members of other third orders, and many simply on a card in their wallet. The classic small rule looks a lot like this camp. Morning: an offering of the day before the phone. Midday: the Angelus when the noon bell rings, or a single Hail Mary. Somewhere in the day, one decade of the rosary, on a walk or in the car. Night: a slow look back at the day, honest, not harsh. Sunday Mass. Confession now and then. That's it. The point of a rule isn't to be heroic. It's to be small enough that you'll actually keep it on a bad Tuesday, and yours enough that you'll want to. Tomorrow a new camp opens: the text itself, starting with the prayer book Benedict's monks prayed seven times a day.
screen: `REGULA: A STRAIGHT STICK.` · `A LITTLE RULE FOR BEGINNERS.` · `MORNING, NOON, A DECADE, NIGHT.` · `SMALL ENOUGH FOR A BAD TUESDAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write your small daily rule. Settle, and breathe. Then choose, from everything this camp offered, just three things. One for the morning. One for sometime in the middle of the day. One for night. Make each one so small it's almost embarrassing: a sign of the cross, one Hail Mary, one minute looking back. If you pray, you can offer the three to God. If you don't, choose three small practices of attention instead. When the bell is done, write them down somewhere you'll see them tomorrow. The bell holds the time.
Regula. Latin for a straight stick, a ruler, a small, steady pattern of prayer for each day, a measuring stick, not a cage. Today's word.
Your line: small, daily, mine. Today, keep the three things you chose, once each, and notice which one was easiest. Day one hundred fifty-six. Camp three is done.

what a scholar hears: regula meant a straightedge, and Benedict's Rule, near its end, calls itself a little rule for beginners.

157.title: How the Psalms work
157.hook: 150 songs of praise, anger, grief and trust, prayed by the Church every day
157.howItsDone: Catholics hear a psalm sung or read at every Mass between the readings, and priests, religious and many lay people pray the psalms daily in the Liturgy of the Hours, at morning, evening and night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rule of life, regula, a measuring stick for the day. Your line was small, daily, mine. Did you keep your three? Today a new camp opens: the text itself. Day one hundred fifty-seven.

Somewhere right now, it's early morning, and a monk in a cold chapel is singing a psalm. Somewhere else it's evening, and a nurse on her break is reading one on her phone. A priest on a train is praying one under his breath. A grieving family in a church hears one read at a funeral. Every single day, all over the world, the Church prays the same book of songs, around the clock. It's the oldest prayer book Christians have, and Jesus prayed from it himself. This camp is about the text, and it starts here.
screen: `A MONK AT DAWN.` → `A NURSE ON HER BREAK.` → `THE SAME BOOK, EVERY DAY.`

segments.voice: The psalter is the Book of Psalms: a hundred and fifty songs. The word comes from Greek. A psalterion was a stringed instrument, and a psalm was a song sung to plucked strings. In Hebrew the book is called Tehillim, praises. But here's the surprise: a great many of them aren't cheerful at all. There are psalms of praise, yes. But there are more psalms of complaint than of anything else: songs that ask God where he's gone, why the wicked win, how long this will last. There are psalms of anger so raw they're hard to read aloud. Psalms of grief, of guilt, of homesickness, of trust in the dark. A bishop in the fourth century, Athanasius of Alexandria, wrote that most of scripture speaks to you, but the psalms speak for you, like a mirror of your own heart. Whatever you're feeling, someone already prayed it. One practical thing before we start reading. The Douay-Rheims follows the old Greek and Latin Bibles, which divide a few psalms differently from the Hebrew. So for most of the book, the Douay number is one lower than a modern Bible's. The famous shepherd psalm is Psalm 23 in most Bibles, and Psalm 22 in the Douay. On this path, the Hebrew number comes in brackets. Catholics meet the psalms all the time: one is sung at every Mass between the readings, and the Liturgy of the Hours, the Church's daily prayer, walks through them morning, evening and night. The book ends on one line: "Let every spirit praise the Lord. Alleluia."
screen: `PSALTERION: STRINGS PLUCKED.` · `MORE COMPLAINTS THAN PRAISES.` · `THEY SPEAK FOR YOU.` · `DOUAY NUMBERS: ONE LOWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open to any psalm and read one verse. If you have a Bible nearby, let it fall open somewhere near the middle; that's usually the Psalms. If you don't, pick any number between one and a hundred and fifty and look it up after the bell. For now, settle and breathe, and ask yourself one honest question: what am I actually feeling today? Tired, grateful, angry, worried, fine. Just name it. Tomorrow the psalms will start to answer. If you pray, you can hold that feeling up to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
Psalter. The Book of Psalms, a hundred and fifty songs for every feeling, prayed by the Church every day. Today's word.
Your line: every feeling has a psalm. Today, when a strong feeling comes, notice it and name it, and remember that someone once sang it to God. Day one hundred fifty-seven.

158.title: Two ways (Psalm 1)
158.hook: a tree planted by running waters, and chaff that blows away
158.howItsDone: Psalm 1 opens the psalter, and Catholics pray it in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it as a responsorial psalm at Mass; many who begin reading the psalms start here, as at a front door.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the psalter, a hundred and fifty songs. Your line was every feeling has a psalm. What feeling did you name? Today, the first psalm, the front door of the book. Day one hundred fifty-eight.

A dry summer. The lawns go brown and the hills turn to straw, but the trees along the river stay green. From a distance you can see where the water runs, because the trees follow it. Their roots found something the rest of the field can't reach. Now the dust at the edge of a parking lot on a windy day, lifting and scattering, landing nowhere. The first psalm, the one that opens the whole book, sets those two pictures side by side and says: there are two ways to live.
screen: `A GREEN TREE IN A DRY SUMMER.` → `DUST ON A WINDY DAY.` → `TWO WAYS.`

segments.voice: Psalm 1 has no title and no author's name. It stands at the entrance like a sign over a door. It opens, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed is the man who hath not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the chair of pestilence." Listen to the verbs: walked, stood, sat. It's a slow slide, from passing by, to stopping, to settling in. Then the other way. That person's will, the Douay says, is in the law of the Lord, "and on his law he shall meditate day and night." The Hebrew word for meditate doesn't mean silent thinking. It means to murmur, to mutter under your breath. It's the same word used for a dove cooing or a lion growling over its catch. Meditating, in the psalms, is saying the words over and over, half aloud, like chewing. And that person, the psalm says, is "like a tree which is planted near the running waters", bearing fruit in its season, its leaf not falling. Notice planted: somebody put it there, on purpose, near the water. Then: "Not so the wicked, not so: but like the dust, which the wind driveth from the face of the earth." In the Hebrew the picture is chaff, the husks blown off the threshing floor. The Latin, and the Douay after it, made it dust. Either way it weighs nothing and has nowhere to land. The psalm doesn't say one way is easy and the other hard. It says one has roots.
screen: `WALKED, STOOD, SAT.` · `MEDITATE: MURMUR IT.` · `A TREE PLANTED BY WATER.` · `DUST THE WIND DRIVES AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand by water, or picture it. If there's a river, a fountain, even a running tap nearby, go to it later. For now, settle and breathe, and imagine a tree on a riverbank. Feel its roots going down, slowly, toward the water under the ground. Then ask: where are my roots drinking from these days? What feeds me, and what just blows through? If you pray, you can murmur one line under your breath, the way the psalm means: blessed is the man. If you don't, just stay with the tree. The bell holds the time.
Two ways. The first psalm's choice: a tree with roots near water, or dust with nowhere to land. Today's word.
Your line: roots near water. Today, do one thing that feeds your roots instead of scattering you, even for five minutes. Day one hundred fifty-eight.

159.title: Sleep in peace (Psalm 4)
159.hook: a psalm for night prayer: in peace I will sleep and I will rest
159.howItsDone: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours pray Psalm 4 at Night Prayer (Compline) on Saturday nights; for centuries it was part of Compline every night, the Church's last prayer before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two ways, and a tree planted by the water. Your line was roots near water. What fed your roots? Today, a psalm for the end of the day. Day one hundred fifty-nine.

It's one in the morning. The house is quiet, and your brain isn't. You're replaying a conversation from this afternoon, the thing they said, the thing you should have said back. You rehearse the perfect reply. Then you rehearse it again. You check the time. You turn the pillow over to the cool side. Long ago, somebody lay awake in a bed like this one, and wrote a song about it. The Church has been singing that song at bedtime for centuries.
screen: `ONE IN THE MORNING.` → `REPLAYING THE CONVERSATION.` → `A SONG FOR THAT BED.`

segments.voice: Psalm 4 is a night psalm. For centuries it was prayed at Compline, the Church's last prayer before sleep, and in today's Liturgy of the Hours it's still there on Saturday nights. It starts in trouble. "When I called upon him, the God of my justice heard me: when I was in distress, thou hast enlarged me." Enlarged: in Hebrew, God made room for me. Distress is a tight place, a narrow corner, and the prayer remembers a time God gave it space. Then comes the line for everyone lying awake angry. In the Douay-Rheims: "Be angry, and sin not: the things you say in your hearts, be sorry for them upon your beds." Notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say don't be angry. It says be angry, and don't let the anger turn into harm. And those speeches you make in your head at one in the morning? The Douay says, be sorry for them upon your beds; the Hebrew says something closer to be still there. Saint Paul quotes the first half of that line to the Ephesians, and adds his own: don't let the sun go down on your anger. The psalm ends with the line the whole night is waiting for: "In peace in the selfsame I will sleep, and I will rest." In the selfsame is an old, hard phrase; it seems to mean at once, or together. Not after everything is fixed. Not after you win the argument. The one praying has the same enemies and the same worries, and still decides to lie down and trust. Sleep, in this psalm, is an act of faith.
screen: `A NIGHT PSALM, PRAYED AT COMPLINE.` · `THOU HAST ENLARGED ME.` · `BE ANGRY, AND SIN NOT.` · `SLEEP AS AN ACT OF TRUST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one line before sleep. Right now, settle and breathe, and find tonight's unfinished conversation, the one most likely to keep you up. Don't solve it. Just notice it, the way the psalm says: say it in your heart, and let it be quiet. Then practice the line you'll say tonight with the light off: in peace I will sleep, and I will rest. If you pray, you can say it to God. If you don't, let it be a way of putting the day down. The bell holds the time.
Sleep in peace. The last line of Psalm 4, a night prayer that lies down before everything is fixed. Today's word.
Your line: in peace I will sleep. Tonight, say it once in the dark, and let tomorrow's arguments wait until tomorrow. Day one hundred fifty-nine.

160.title: What is man (Psalm 8)
160.hook: the stars, and yet God is mindful of us
160.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 8 in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it at Mass, including on the feast of the Holy Trinity in some years; the Letter to the Hebrews applies its words to Jesus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a night psalm that lies down before anything is fixed. Your line was in peace I will sleep. Did you say it in the dark? Tonight, look up. Day one hundred sixty.

A farm road at night, far from any town. The car door shuts, the headlights go off, and someone looks up. There are far too many stars. The Milky Way is a smear of light across the whole sky. All of that, and here's one person, standing on a patch of gravel with cold hands. Someone stood under that same sky, without telescopes, without knowing how far away any of it was, and asked the question out loud.
screen: `FAR TOO MANY STARS.` → `ONE PERSON ON THE GRAVEL.`

segments.voice: Psalm 8 opens and closes with nearly the same line, like two hands cupped around it: "O Lord our Lord, how admirable is thy name in the whole earth!" In between, the question. "For I will behold thy heavens, the works of thy fingers: the moon and the stars which thou hast founded." Fingers. Not arms, not great labor: the whole night sky as fingerwork, like embroidery. And then: "What is man that thou art mindful of him? or the son of man that thou visitest him?" The Hebrew word for man here, enosh, has the sense of a frail human, someone mortal and breakable. The question isn't philosophical. It's astonished. Why would the one who made all that bother to remember this? And then the psalm turns the smallness inside out: "Thou hast made him a little less than the angels, thou hast crowned him with glory and honour." One detail in the Hebrew. The Hebrew says a little less than elohim, a word that can mean God, or gods, or heavenly beings. The old Greek translators chose angels, the Latin and the Douay followed, and the Letter to the Hebrews quotes it that way about Jesus. The Church reads both: every human being small, and crowned. In 1969 the Apollo 11 astronauts left a small disc on the moon with messages from world leaders, and Pope Paul VI's words on it quoted this psalm. The words went all the way up to the thing the psalm was looking at.
screen: `THE WORK OF THY FINGERS.` · `WHAT IS MAN?` · `A LITTLE LESS THAN THE ANGELS.` · `THE PSALM WENT TO THE MOON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the night sky tonight. If it's night where you are, step outside or go to a window now. If it's daytime, close your eyes and remember the darkest, starriest sky you've ever seen. Settle, and breathe. Notice how big it is, and how small one person is beside it. Don't hurry past it. Then hold the other half of the psalm alongside it: small, and still remembered. If you pray, you can say the psalm's first line, O Lord our Lord. If you don't, just stay with the size of things. The bell holds the time.
Enosh. Hebrew for a frail, mortal human, the psalm's word for the question under the stars: why would God remember someone so small? Today's word.
Your line: small, and remembered. Tonight, look up for one full minute, and let yourself be both. Day one hundred sixty.

161.title: The heavens shew forth (Psalm 18 [19])
161.hook: the sky speaks without words, and the law is sweeter than honey
161.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 18 [19] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear its second half at Mass, often as the responsorial psalm answering a reading about God's law.

segments.voice: Yesterday, what is man, enosh, under a sky full of stars. Your line was small, and remembered. Did you look up? Today the sky gets a voice, and the week closes. Day one hundred sixty-one.

A sunset over a highway. A driver pulls onto the shoulder and holds up a phone, and the picture comes out flat and useless. The phone goes back in a pocket, and the driver just looks. Nobody says anything. There aren't any words. And yet it's as if something has been said. A poet in ancient Israel had that same feeling and wrote it down, and then did something unexpected: he put the sky and a book side by side.
screen: `A SUNSET ON THE SHOULDER.` → `NO WORDS, BUT SOMETHING SAID.`

segments.voice: Psalm 18 in the Douay, 19 in most Bibles, opens: "The heavens shew forth the glory of God, and the firmament declareth the work of his hands." Shew is just the old spelling of show. And the firmament is the great dome of the sky; the Hebrew word pictures something hammered flat, like beaten metal. Then: "Day to day uttereth speech, and night to night sheweth knowledge." Each day hands the news on to the next, like a relay. And yet: "There are no speeches nor languages, where their voices are not heard." The sky speaks in no language, which means everyone on earth can hear it. Then the psalm pictures the sun coming out each morning like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, rejoicing like a giant to run his way, and nothing hidden from its heat. And then, halfway through, it turns. Suddenly it's not about the sky at all. It's about the law of the Lord, God's teaching: it converts souls, gives wisdom to little ones, rejoices hearts. The commandments are "more to be desired than gold and many precious stones: and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb." Why put these together? An old Christian image speaks of two books, creation and scripture. In that picture, the sky shows that there is glory, and the page names whose it is. And after both, the psalm ends small and personal, asking to be cleansed of hidden faults, and that the words of the mouth and the thoughts of the heart would be pleasing. This week took us from the saints' calendar to a rule of life to the first psalms. Here the sky and the page meet.

If you pray, you can end with the psalm's first line: the heavens shew forth the glory of God. If you don't, simply let the sky be enough. The bell holds the time.
